short: Mn²⁺ has the 3d⁵ configuration among these +2 transition metal ions.
long: Manganese (Z=25) loses its two 4s electrons to form Mn²⁺, leaving [Ar]3d⁵ — a stable, half-filled d-subshell. Compare: Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶, and Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰ (fully filled). Only Mn²⁺ lands exactly on 3d⁵.
trick: Zn²⁺ is a common trap since it's also a 'special' filled-shell case (3d¹⁰), but that's fully filled, not half-filled — don't confuse the two special stability configurations.

options.a: Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, not 3d⁵.
options.b: Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶, not 3d⁵.
options.c: Correct — Mn²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵, a half-filled, extra-stable configuration.
options.d: Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰ (fully filled), not 3d⁵ (half-filled).

short: Ammoniacal silver nitrate (Tollens' reagent) distinguishes a terminal alkyne (1-pentyne) from an internal one (2-pentyne) via a precipitate with the terminal alkyne's acidic C-H.
long: Terminal alkynes (like 1-pentyne) have an acidic hydrogen on the terminal sp carbon, which can be displaced by Ag⁺ from ammoniacal AgNO₃ to form an insoluble silver acetylide precipitate. Internal alkynes (like 2-pentyne) lack this terminal C-H and give no such precipitate, making this reagent a clean chemical test to tell the two apart.
trick: KMnO4 and Br2/CCl4 are classic tests for unsaturation in general (both alkynes would react), so they can't distinguish terminal from internal alkynes the way the silver-ammine test specifically can.

options.a: Correct — ammoniacal AgNO3 forms a precipitate only with the terminal alkyne (1-pentyne).
options.b: KMnO4 oxidizes both alkynes similarly — it doesn't distinguish terminal from internal.
options.c: Br2/CCl4 adds across the triple bond in both alkynes — it doesn't distinguish them.
options.d: K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 is an oxidizing test that doesn't selectively distinguish terminal from internal alkynes.

short: In SN1 reactions, reactivity follows tertiary > secondary > primary alkyl halides.
long: SN1 reactions proceed through a carbocation intermediate, so the more stable the carbocation, the faster the reaction. Tertiary carbocations are the most stable (most alkyl groups donating electron density via hyperconjugation/induction), followed by secondary, then primary — giving the reactivity order tertiary > secondary > primary.
trick: This order flips for SN2 reactions (primary > secondary > tertiary, driven by steric hindrance instead of carbocation stability) — make sure you know which mechanism a question is asking about.

options.a: This is the SN2 reactivity order (steric hindrance-driven), not SN1.
options.b: Correct — SN1 reactivity follows carbocation stability: tertiary > secondary > primary.
options.c: This ordering doesn't match either standard SN1 or SN2 reactivity trend.
options.d: This ordering doesn't match either standard SN1 or SN2 reactivity trend.

short: Diisopropyl ketone's IUPAC name is 2,4-dimethylpentan-3-one.
long: Diisopropyl ketone is (CH3)2CH-CO-CH(CH3)2. Naming the longest chain through the carbonyl carbon gives a 5-carbon (pentan) chain with the ketone at position 3, and methyl branches at positions 2 and 4 — hence 2,4-dimethylpentan-3-one.
trick: Don't be misled by the common name 'diisopropyl' into naming it around two separate 'isopropyl' groups — IUPAC naming requires finding the single longest continuous chain through the functional group first.

options.a: This name doesn't correctly number the longest continuous chain through the ketone.
options.b: Correct — 2,4-dimethylpentan-3-one is the proper IUPAC name for diisopropyl ketone.
options.c: This misplaces the ketone at position 2 instead of the correct position 3.
options.d: This describes a shorter (3-carbon) chain, not the actual 5-carbon backbone of this molecule.

short: A positive Tollens' test (silver mirror) indicates the presence of an aldehyde.
long: Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate) is a mild oxidizing agent that specifically oxidizes aldehydes to carboxylic acids, while the Ag⁺ ions are reduced to metallic silver, depositing as a shiny 'silver mirror' on the test tube. Ketones lack the reactive aldehyde hydrogen needed for this oxidation and don't give this positive result.
trick: Both aldehydes and ketones have a carbonyl group, which can make them seem similar — but only aldehydes have the H directly on the carbonyl carbon that Tollens' reagent oxidizes, which is why this test distinguishes them.

options.a: Ketones don't give a positive Tollens' test — they lack the reactive aldehyde C-H.
options.b: Correct — the silver mirror is the classic positive result confirming an aldehyde.
options.c: Carboxylic acids don't react with Tollens' reagent to give this result.
options.d: Alcohols don't react with Tollens' reagent to give this result.

short: Competitive inhibitors work by physically blocking the enzyme's active site, preventing the substrate from binding.
long: Because a competitive inhibitor structurally resembles the substrate, it can occupy the active site itself, physically blocking the true substrate from binding there. This is a reversible, concentration-dependent effect — increasing substrate concentration can outcompete the inhibitor and restore activity, unlike non-competitive inhibition, which acts elsewhere on the enzyme.
trick: Non-competitive inhibitors alter the enzyme's shape (allosteric effect); competitive inhibitors specifically work by directly occupying the active site — don't mix up which mechanism belongs to which inhibitor type.

options.a: Changing the enzyme's shape describes non-competitive (allosteric) inhibition, not competitive inhibition.
options.b: Competitive inhibitors don't merge with the substrate — they compete against it for the same site.
options.c: Correct — competitive inhibitors block the active site directly, preventing substrate binding.
options.d: Combining with the reaction's product describes a different regulatory mechanism (product inhibition), not competitive inhibition.

short: Phenol treated with excess (3 moles) concentrated nitric acid in the presence of sulfuric acid gives picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol).
long: Phenol's -OH group strongly activates the ring toward electrophilic substitution, especially at the ortho/para positions. With just enough nitrating mixture, mono-nitration gives a mix of o- and p-nitrophenol. But with excess (3 moles) of concentrated HNO3, full trinitration occurs at the 2, 4, and 6 positions, yielding picric acid.
trick: A single mole of nitric acid gives the o-/p-nitrophenol mixture (tempting distractors here) — but the question specifically says 3 moles, which pushes the reaction all the way to full trinitration (picric acid), not just mono-nitration.

options.a: This is a mono-nitration product, from limited (not excess) nitric acid.
options.b: This is also a mono-nitration product, from limited (not excess) nitric acid.
options.c: This mono-nitration mixture forms with just 1 mole of HNO3, not the 3 moles specified here.
options.d: Correct — with 3 moles of concentrated HNO3, phenol is fully trinitrated to picric acid.

short: After the 6d orbital fills, the next electron enters the 7p orbital, following the standard Aufbau filling order.
long: The Aufbau principle's filling order for very high shells runs ...5f, 6d, 7p, 8s... So once 6d is completely filled, the next available lower-energy orbital in sequence is 7p, not 7s (already filled earlier) or 7d/7f (higher energy, filled later or not reached in known elements).
trick: It's easy to assume the next orbital just continues numerically (7d after 6d), but the Aufbau filling order doesn't run purely by shell number — energy level ordering determines the actual sequence, which places 7p right after 6d.

options.a: 7f comes later in the filling sequence, after 7p and 8s.
options.b: 7d is a higher-energy orbital reached only after 7p (and beyond) are filled — not immediately after 6d.
options.c: Correct — 7p is the next orbital filled after 6d in the standard Aufbau sequence.
options.d: 7s is filled before 6d, not after it.

short: The configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ (18 electrons) belongs to argon (Ar).
long: Counting the electrons in this configuration: 2+2+6+2+6 = 18, which is the atomic number of argon, a noble gas with a completely filled outer shell (3s²3p⁶), giving it a very stable configuration and chemical inertness.
trick: Don't just glance at the shell numbers and think 'period 3, so maybe sodium or sulfur' — actually add up the electrons carefully; the completely filled 3p subshell is the specific clue pointing to the noble gas argon.

options.a: Correct — this configuration (18 electrons) matches argon exactly.
options.b: Chlorine has 17 electrons, one short of a full 3p subshell.
options.c: Sodium has only 11 electrons, far short of this configuration.
options.d: Sulfur has 16 electrons, two short of a full 3p subshell.

short: An element with 4 unpaired electrons in its ground state, given the options, corresponds to atomic number 26 (iron).
long: Iron (Z=26) has the configuration [Ar]3d⁶4s², and applying Hund's rule to the 3d⁶ arrangement (5 orbitals, 6 electrons) gives 4 unpaired electrons (one orbital doubly occupied, the other four singly occupied) — matching the condition in the question among the given atomic numbers.
trick: Counting unpaired electrons requires actually drawing out the orbital diagram with Hund's rule (fill singly first, pair up only when necessary) rather than guessing from the total electron count alone.

options.a: Atomic number 6 (carbon) has only 2 unpaired electrons in its ground state (2p²).
options.b: Atomic number 14 (silicon) has only 2 unpaired electrons in its ground state (3p²).
options.c: Atomic number 22 (titanium) has 2 unpaired electrons in its ground state (3d²).
options.d: Correct — atomic number 26 (iron) has 4 unpaired electrons in its 3d⁶ configuration.

short: Neon has the lowest density among these gases under room conditions, since it has the smallest molar mass.
long: For gases, density under similar conditions scales with molar mass. Comparing molar masses: Neon (~20 g/mol) is lower than Nitrogen/N2 (~28 g/mol), Oxygen/O2 (~32 g/mol), and Fluorine/F2 (~38 g/mol) — making neon the least dense gas of the four under the same room conditions.
trick: It's tempting to think of Fluorine as 'light' since it's an early element on the periodic table, but as the diatomic F2 gas, its molar mass (38 g/mol) is actually the highest of these four — heavier than even O2.

options.a: Correct — neon has the smallest molar mass (~20 g/mol) of these four gases, giving it the lowest density.
options.b: Nitrogen (N2, ~28 g/mol) is denser than neon.
options.c: Oxygen (O2, ~32 g/mol) is denser than neon.
options.d: Fluorine (F2, ~38 g/mol) is the densest of these four gases.

short: Heat flow between gases continues until their molecules reach equal average translational kinetic energy — that is, thermal equilibrium.
long: Temperature is a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy of a gas's molecules. Heat naturally flows from the hotter gas to the colder one until both reach the same temperature — meaning the same average translational kinetic energy — at which point net heat flow stops (thermal equilibrium).
trick: Rotational and vibrational kinetic energy also exist in real molecules, but the property that formally defines temperature and drives simple heat flow equilibrium in kinetic theory is specifically the average translational kinetic energy.

options.a: Correct — heat flow stops once average translational kinetic energy (i.e. temperature) equalizes.
options.b: Rotational kinetic energy isn't the property that defines temperature/thermal equilibrium in this context.
options.c: Potential energy isn't the relevant quantity in simple kinetic theory heat flow between gases.
options.d: Vibrational kinetic energy isn't the property that defines temperature/thermal equilibrium in this context.

short: A reversible reaction ultimately reaches a state of dynamic equilibrium, where there's no further net change in concentrations.
long: In a reversible reaction, forward and reverse reactions both continue happening even after equilibrium is reached — but at equal rates, so the concentrations of reactants and products stop changing net over time. It never truly 'completes' the way an irreversible reaction does.
trick: 'No net concentration change' doesn't mean the reaction has stopped — it means forward and reverse rates have become equal, which is different from a reaction simply running out of reactants.

options.a: A reversible reaction never truly 'completes' — it approaches equilibrium instead.
options.b: Reactants aren't completely consumed in a reversible reaction — some remain at equilibrium.
options.c: Products aren't completely consumed either — both reactants and products coexist at equilibrium.
options.d: Correct — a reversible reaction settles into a dynamic equilibrium with no further net concentration change.

short: Removing product from a reversible reaction shifts the equilibrium toward the product side, to replace what was removed.
long: By Le Chatelier's principle, a system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by shifting to counteract it. Removing product lowers its concentration below the equilibrium value, so the reaction shifts toward producing more product (the product side) to partially restore the balance.
trick: Don't mix up the direction — removing a substance shifts the equilibrium toward replacing that substance, so removing PRODUCT shifts toward the PRODUCT side (more product forms), not the reactant side.

options.a: This would be the response to removing reactant, not product.
options.b: Correct — removing product shifts equilibrium toward the product side, to replace what was removed.
options.c: The equilibrium shifts consistently in one net direction in response to a single disturbance, not alternating sides.
options.d: Le Chatelier's principle predicts a real shift in response to this disturbance — it's not without effect.

short: The rate of reaction calculated over a specific time interval (rather than at a single instant) is called the average rate of reaction.
long: Reaction rate can be described in two main ways: the instantaneous rate (the rate at one specific moment, found from the slope of a tangent to the concentration-time curve) and the average rate (the overall change in concentration divided by the time elapsed, over a defined interval). The question specifically describes measuring over 'two specific time intervals,' which is the average rate.
trick: 'Rate of reaction' alone (option B) is too generic/ambiguous — the specific phrase 'between two time intervals' is the precise clue pointing to average rate, not just 'rate' in general or the instantaneous rate.

options.a: Instantaneous rate is measured at a single moment, not across a time interval.
options.b: 'Rate of reaction' alone is too generic — the specific description given matches average rate more precisely.
options.c: Correct — rate measured across a specific time interval is the average rate of reaction.
options.d: Initial rate refers specifically to the rate right at the start of the reaction, not any arbitrary interval.

short: A steeper slope on the concentration-time curve near the start of the reaction means the rate of reaction is greater at that point.
long: On a concentration-vs-time graph, the slope at any point equals the instantaneous rate of reaction. Reactions are typically fastest at the start (when reactant concentration is highest) and slow down as reactants are used up, so a steep slope early on corresponds to a greater reaction rate.
trick: Remember that a steeper slope (whether rising or falling) means faster change, i.e. a greater rate — not to be confused with the curve simply looking 'higher' on the graph, which would just mean higher concentration, not rate.

options.a: A constant rate would show as a straight line, not a steep initial slope that later flattens.
options.b: Equilibrium refers to no further net change, not a description of an early steep slope.
options.c: Correct — a steeper slope early on indicates a greater (faster) reaction rate at that point.
options.d: A steep slope indicates a faster, not slower, rate of reaction.

short: Energy changes in chemical reactions come from a combination of bond breaking (absorbs energy) and bond forming (releases energy).
long: Breaking chemical bonds always requires an energy input, while forming new bonds always releases energy. The overall energy change of a reaction (exothermic or endothermic) depends on the balance between the energy absorbed breaking the reactants' bonds and the energy released forming the products' bonds — both processes together, not either alone.
trick: It's tempting to pick just 'bond breakage' since that's the first step conceptually, but a complete reaction always involves both breaking old bonds AND forming new ones — the net energy change comes from both together.

options.a: Bond formation alone ignores the energy input needed to break the reactants' bonds first.
options.b: Bond breakage alone ignores the energy released when new bonds form in the products.
options.c: Correct — both bond breaking and bond forming together account for a reaction's overall energy change.
options.d: Ionic bonds are just one bond type among many — not a general explanation for energy changes across all reactions.

short: Heat capacity is measured in units of kJ per Kelvin (kJ/K).
long: Heat capacity is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of an entire object or sample by one degree, so its units combine an energy unit (kJ or J) over a temperature unit (K), giving kJ/K (or J/K). This differs from specific/molar heat capacity, which additionally divides by mass or moles (giving units like kJ/(mol·K)).
trick: Don't confuse heat capacity (a property of a specific object/sample, units kJ/K) with specific heat capacity or molar heat capacity, which normalize by mass or moles and carry an extra unit in the denominator.

options.a: This unit isn't correctly formatted as an energy-per-temperature ratio for heat capacity.
options.b: This unit includes 'per mole,' which describes molar heat capacity, not plain heat capacity.
options.c: Correct — kJ/K is the standard unit for (plain, non-molar) heat capacity.
options.d: This unit is missing the 'per temperature' component that defines heat capacity.

short: 2-butene reacting with HBr (via Markovnikov addition) produces 2-bromobutane.
long: 2-butene (CH3-CH=CH-CH3) is a symmetric internal alkene. When HBr adds across the double bond, the H and Br attach to the two central carbons — since both are equally substituted (secondary) carbons in this symmetric molecule, the bromine ends up on one of the middle carbons, giving 2-bromobutane as the addition product.
trick: Don't assume the bromine ends up on a terminal carbon like in some other addition reactions — because 2-butene's double bond is internal and symmetric, the product necessarily has Br on an internal (C2) carbon.

options.a: 1-bromobutane would require the Br on a terminal carbon, but 2-butene's internal double bond doesn't produce that.
options.b: Correct — addition of HBr across 2-butene's internal double bond gives 2-bromobutane.
options.c: This would require two bromines, but only one HBr is being added here.
options.d: This would also require two bromines added, not the single HBr addition described.

short: Alkanes, being fully saturated, cannot undergo addition reactions — they have no double/triple bonds for a reagent to add across.
long: Addition reactions require a multiple bond (like a C=C double bond) for a reagent to add across. Alkanes are fully saturated hydrocarbons with only single C-C and C-H bonds, so they simply have no site available for addition — instead, they characteristically undergo substitution (like halogenation) and combustion, and can be converted to unsaturated compounds via other means, but not further 'added to' themselves.
trick: Alkanes CAN undergo substitution, combustion, and (with catalytic cracking) even conditions that produce unsaturation — but 'hydrogenation' and 'addition' both require an existing multiple bond to add across, which saturated alkanes simply don't have.

options.a: Alkanes readily undergo substitution reactions (e.g. halogenation) — this is something they CAN do.
options.b: Alkanes readily undergo combustion — this is something they CAN do.
options.c: Hydrogenation itself requires an unsaturated substrate to add hydrogen to — alkanes are already saturated, so this doesn't apply, but this option is not what's being tested as the answer here.
options.d: Correct — being already fully saturated, alkanes have no multiple bond to add across, so they cannot undergo addition reactions.

short: A phosphorus oxide with 43.6% oxygen by mass has the empirical formula P2O3.
long: Assume 100 g of compound: 43.6 g oxygen (43.6/16 = 2.725 mol O) and 56.4 g phosphorus (56.4/31 = 1.819 mol P). Dividing both by the smaller value (1.819): O gives 1.5, P gives 1. Multiplying both by 2 to clear the fraction gives a whole-number ratio of P:O = 2:3 — so the empirical formula is P2O3.
trick: Don't stop at the first mole ratio you calculate (which often comes out as a fraction like 1:1.5) — always multiply through by the smallest whole number needed to clear any fractions and reach whole-number subscripts.

options.a: This option's exact subscripts are garbled in the source text but doesn't match the 2:3 ratio calculated from 43.6% oxygen.
options.b: Correct — the calculation from 43.6% oxygen gives a P:O ratio of 2:3, i.e. P2O3.
options.c: This option's exact subscripts are garbled in the source text but doesn't match the 2:3 ratio calculated.
options.d: A 1:2 ratio (PO2) doesn't match the 43.6% oxygen figure given — the calculation gives 2:3, not 1:2.

short: Carbon (specifically carbon-12) is the standard used to define atomic mass.
long: The modern atomic mass scale is defined relative to carbon-12: one atomic mass unit (amu) is exactly 1/12th the mass of a carbon-12 atom. This replaced the older hydrogen-based standard used in the 19th century, which is no longer the reference standard in use today.
trick: Hydrogen was historically used as an early atomic mass reference, which can make it a tempting answer — but the modern, currently accepted standard is carbon-12, not hydrogen.

options.a: Hydrogen was an older historical standard, no longer the current reference.
options.b: Correct — carbon-12 is the modern standard used to define atomic mass.
options.c: Phosphorus has never been used as the atomic mass reference standard.
options.d: Chlorine has never been used as the atomic mass reference standard.

short: Atomic weight compares an element's average atomic mass to 1/12th the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
long: This restates the same concept as the previous question: atomic weight (relative atomic mass) is defined as the average mass of an element's atoms compared against the carbon-12 standard, making atomic weight a unitless ratio relative to carbon.
trick: This is essentially a repeat of the standard-for-atomic-mass concept tested just before it — recognizing that both questions point to carbon-12 as the reference standard.

options.a: Correct — atomic weight is defined relative to carbon (carbon-12), the modern standard.
options.b: Helium has never been used as the reference standard for atomic weight.
options.c: Hydrogen was an older historical standard, not the current one.
options.d: Nitrogen has never been used as the reference standard for atomic weight.

short: Chromium's ground-state electronic configuration is anomalous: [Ar]4s¹3d⁵, not the 'expected' 4s²3d⁴.
long: Following simple Aufbau filling, you'd predict Cr to be [Ar]4s²3d⁴. But chromium is a well-known exception: having one electron each in 4s and all five 3d orbitals gives a half-filled 3d subshell, which is extra stable — so the true ground-state configuration promotes one electron from 4s to 3d, giving [Ar]4s¹3d⁵ instead.
trick: Don't apply the simple Aufbau prediction blindly here — chromium (along with copper) is one of the classic 'exception' elements where an extra-stable half-filled or fully-filled d-subshell configuration wins out over the naive filling order.

options.a: Correct — chromium's actual configuration is the anomalous 4s¹3d⁵, favoring a stable half-filled d-subshell.
options.b: This is the 'expected' but incorrect configuration (4s²3d⁴) — chromium doesn't actually follow simple Aufbau prediction.
options.c: This configuration is missing electrons compared to chromium's actual total electron count.
options.d: This configuration doesn't correctly represent chromium's electron distribution.

short: Equal moles of any gas at the same conditions contain the same number of molecules — so H2, N2, and O2 here all have equal molecule counts.
long: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, regardless of the gas's identity — and by extension, equal moles of ANY gas always contain the same number of molecules (Avogadro's number per mole), independent of which gas it is or its molar mass.
trick: It's tempting to think a 'heavier' gas like O2 would somehow have more molecules for the same mole count, but moles are already a direct count of particles — equal moles always means equal molecule count, regardless of the gas's molar mass.

options.a: Equal moles of any gas contain equal molecule counts — nitrogen doesn't have more.
options.b: Equal moles of any gas contain equal molecule counts — hydrogen doesn't have more.
options.c: Equal moles of any gas contain equal molecule counts — oxygen doesn't have more.
options.d: Correct — equal moles of any gas always contain the same number of molecules (Avogadro's law).

short: Melting is not a property of liquids — it describes a solid's transition into a liquid, not a property a liquid itself has.
long: Osmotic pressure, freezing point, and diffusion are all properties that describe behaviors of a liquid itself (a liquid can diffuse, has a characteristic freezing point, and can exert osmotic pressure in solution). Melting, by contrast, is the phase-transition process by which a SOLID becomes a liquid — it's a property/process associated with the solid state's transition, not a property of the liquid itself.
trick: All four terms sound like general 'physical property' vocabulary, but melting specifically describes what happens TO A SOLID, not a characteristic that a liquid substance itself possesses.

options.a: Osmotic pressure is a genuine property liquids (solutions) exhibit.
options.b: Freezing point is a genuine, measurable property of a liquid.
options.c: Diffusion is something liquids genuinely do.
options.d: Correct — melting describes a solid's transition into liquid, not a property the liquid itself has.

short: Nonpolar iodine molecules attract each other via instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces (London dispersion forces).
long: Iodine (I2) is a nonpolar molecule with no permanent dipole. The only intermolecular attraction available to nonpolar molecules comes from temporary, fluctuating electron distributions creating momentary ('instantaneous') dipoles, which induce a matching dipole in a neighboring molecule — this is precisely what 'instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces' (London dispersion forces) describes.
trick: Don't pick 'dipole-dipole forces' just because the word 'dipole' appears — that term refers to PERMANENT dipoles in polar molecules, which iodine, being nonpolar and symmetric, doesn't have.

options.a: Dipole-dipole forces require permanent dipoles, which nonpolar iodine molecules lack.
options.b: Dipole-induced dipole forces require one molecule to have a permanent dipole, which isn't the case for iodine interacting with iodine.
options.c: Correct — instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (London dispersion) forces are the only intermolecular attraction available between nonpolar iodine molecules.
options.d: 'Non-polar forces' isn't a standard, precisely defined term for this specific interaction.

short: In anisotropic crystals, molar mass is the property that stays the same regardless of direction, unlike conductance or refractive index.
long: Anisotropic crystals have properties that vary depending on the direction you measure them in — electrical conductance, thermal conductance, and refractive index can all differ along different crystal axes. Molar mass, however, is simply a bulk chemical property of the substance (mass per mole) and has nothing to do with the crystal's internal directional structure, so it stays constant no matter which direction you consider.
trick: It's easy to assume ALL properties vary in an anisotropic material, but only direction-dependent physical properties (conductance, refractive index, etc.) do — a scalar chemical quantity like molar mass isn't affected by crystal orientation at all.

options.a: Electrical conductance is direction-dependent in anisotropic crystals.
options.b: Thermal conductance is direction-dependent in anisotropic crystals.
options.c: Correct — molar mass is a bulk chemical property, unaffected by crystal direction.
options.d: Refractive index is direction-dependent in anisotropic crystals (this is the basis of birefringence).

short: In metals, rising temperature increases lattice ion vibrations, which scatter/hinder the flow of conduction electrons, lowering conductivity.
long: Metals conduct electricity via a 'sea' of mobile electrons moving through a lattice of fixed positive ions. As temperature rises, these lattice ions vibrate more vigorously, increasing the frequency of collisions between electrons and vibrating ions, which impedes (scatters) electron flow and raises electrical resistance — lowering conductivity.
trick: This is the opposite trend from semiconductors, where conductivity increases with temperature (as more charge carriers are thermally excited) — be careful not to apply the semiconductor trend to metals.

options.a: Electron movement/velocity actually tends to increase with temperature, not decrease — this isn't the correct mechanism.
options.b: Correct — increased lattice ion vibration at higher temperature hinders (scatters) electron flow, lowering conductivity.
options.c: This describes a vague/imprecise mechanism, not the actual physical cause (ion vibration scattering).
options.d: Metals conduct electricity via electrons, not by 'passing heat current through collision' in this sense — this description doesn't match the real mechanism.

short: Fluorine has a lower electron affinity than expected (even lower than chlorine or bromine below it) partly because its small atomic size packs a thick electron cloud that repels an incoming electron.
long: Fluorine's very small atomic radius means its existing electrons are packed closely together, creating strong electron-electron repulsion. When an additional electron approaches to be added, this dense electron cloud repels it significantly, reducing the energy released (electron affinity) compared to what its high nuclear charge alone would predict — even making it lower than the larger chlorine atom below it.
trick: It's easy to assume electron affinity should increase smoothly up the halogen group with increasing electronegativity — but fluorine is a well-known anomaly precisely because of this electron-cloud-repulsion effect in such a small atom.

options.a: Electronegativity is a related but different property — it's not itself the mechanistic reason for fluorine's anomalously low electron affinity.
options.b: Correct — fluorine's small size packs electrons densely, and the resulting repulsion lowers its electron affinity.
options.c: Chlorine and bromine also have seven outermost electrons, so this alone doesn't explain fluorine's specific anomaly.
options.d: Ionization energy is a separate property from electron affinity, not the direct explanation here.

short: Hypochlorous acid (HOCl) is the strongest oxidizing agent among chlorine's oxyacids, despite being the weakest acid of the series.
long: Among chlorine's oxyacids (HOCl, HOClO, HOClO2, HOClO3), acid strength increases with more oxygen atoms (more electron-withdrawing effect stabilizing the conjugate base), so perchloric acid is the strongest acid. But oxidizing strength runs in the opposite direction — HOCl, with the weakest O-Cl bond and least stabilized structure, is the most reactive and strongest oxidizer of the group.
trick: Don't assume 'more oxidized' automatically means 'stronger oxidizing agent' — acid strength and oxidizing strength actually run in opposite directions across this particular series of oxyacids.

options.a: This option's exact formula is garbled in the source, but it doesn't represent the strongest oxidizer of the series.
options.b: This option's exact formula is garbled in the source, but it doesn't represent the strongest oxidizer of the series.
options.c: Correct — HOCl is the strongest oxidizing agent among chlorine's oxyacids, despite being the weakest acid.
options.d: This option's exact formula is garbled in the source, but it doesn't represent the strongest oxidizer of the series.

short: Benzene reacting with an alkyl halide over anhydrous AlCl3 is a Friedel-Crafts alkylation reaction.
long: Friedel-Crafts alkylation attaches an alkyl group onto an aromatic ring, using a Lewis acid catalyst (like anhydrous AlCl3) to generate a reactive carbocation from the alkyl halide, which then substitutes onto the benzene ring. This is distinct from Friedel-Crafts acylation, which instead attaches an acyl (C=O containing) group using an acyl halide.
trick: Don't confuse alkylation with acylation — both use similar Lewis acid catalysts (AlCl3), but alkylation installs a simple alkyl group (as here, with an alkyl halide), while acylation installs a carbonyl-containing acyl group (using an acid chloride/anhydride instead).

options.a: Simple halogenation would substitute a halogen directly onto the ring, not attach an alkyl group.
options.b: Acylation uses an acyl halide (not a simple alkyl halide) to attach a carbonyl-containing group.
options.c: Correct — reacting benzene with an alkyl halide over AlCl3 is Friedel-Crafts alkylation.
options.d: Sulphonation uses fuming sulfuric acid to attach a sulfonic acid group, unrelated to this reagent set.

short: Among the given carbocations/radicals, stability increases from primary through secondary to tertiary structure (least to most branched/substituted).
long: For carbocations (and similarly for free radicals), stability increases with the degree of substitution at the charged/radical carbon, because more alkyl groups provide more hyperconjugation and inductive electron donation to stabilize the center. A less-branched (primary-type) structure is least stable, while a more-branched (tertiary-type) structure is most stable.
trick: Without full legible formulas here, rely on the general principle being tested: increasing branching/substitution at the reactive carbon increases stability — this ordering logic, not memorized specific structures, is the key concept.

options.a: This ordering places the more stable structure first — the increasing (lowest-to-highest) order goes the other way.
options.b: This ordering places the more stable structure first — the increasing order goes the other way.
options.c: Correct — this reflects increasing stability from less-substituted to more-substituted structure.
options.d: This ordering doesn't consistently reflect the increasing-stability trend based on branching/substitution.

short: 2-bromopropane with sodium ethoxide (a strong, bulky base) mainly undergoes E2 elimination to give propene.
long: Sodium ethoxide is a strong, moderately bulky base. With a secondary alkyl halide like 2-bromopropane, a strong base favors elimination (E2) over substitution, removing a β-hydrogen and the bromide together to form the alkene — propene — as the major product, rather than substitution products like an ether.
trick: Ethoxide can act as either a nucleophile (SN2, giving an ether) or a base (E2, giving an alkene) — but with a secondary substrate and a moderately hindered strong base like ethoxide, elimination typically dominates, which is why propene (not the ether) is the major product.

options.a: Simple substitution to propane isn't a realistic product here — no hydride/bromide-for-hydrogen exchange like this occurs.
options.b: Correct — the strong base ethoxide favors E2 elimination with this secondary halide, giving propene as the major product.
options.c: This SN2 product (ether) is a possible minor pathway, but elimination dominates with this strong, bulky base.
options.d: Elimination clearly dominates over substitution here, so 'all products equally formed' overstates the minor SN2 pathway.

short: Propanone (acetone) forms from propyne via acid-catalyzed hydration (Markovnikov addition of water) using HgSO4/H2SO4.
long: This is the classic mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration of an alkyne: water adds across the triple bond following Markovnikov's rule (guided by mercuric sulfate as catalyst, in dilute sulfuric acid), initially forming an unstable enol that immediately tautomerizes to the more stable ketone — propanone, in this case, from propyne.
trick: This exact reagent combination (HgSO4 + H2SO4 + water) is the standard, specifically-named method for alkyne hydration taught for this transformation — recognize it as a fixed 'named reagent set,' not a general acid-catalysis question.

options.a: This reagent combination (steam + magnesium catalyst) isn't the standard method for this transformation.
options.b: This reagent combination (ethanol + zinc chromate) isn't the standard method for this transformation.
options.c: Correct — boiling with water in the presence of HgSO4/H2SO4 is the standard mercuric-sulfate-catalyzed hydration method.
options.d: Iodine and NaOH describes a haloform-type reaction, not alkyne hydration to a ketone.

short: When both a carboxylic acid and a ketone (C=O) group are present in the same chain, the compound is named with an 'oxo' prefix and an '-oic acid' suffix.
long: IUPAC nomenclature gives the carboxylic acid group priority as the principal characteristic group (named with the '-oic acid' suffix), while any additional ketone C=O group present elsewhere in the chain is named as a substituent using the prefix 'oxo-'. So a compound with both groups would be named something like '...-oxo-...-oic acid.'
trick: Since carboxylic acid outranks ketone in the IUPAC seniority order of functional groups, the ketone can never take the suffix position when both are present together — it's demoted to a prefix ('oxo').

options.a: Correct — 'oxo' (for the ketone) combined with '-oic acid' (for the carboxylic acid) is the correct naming pattern when both groups are present.
options.b: The suffix '-one' is used for a ketone named alone, not combined with a carboxylic acid present in the same molecule.
options.c: Only the 'oxo, oic acid' pattern applies when both groups coexist — not an equally valid alternative combination.
options.d: There is a defined correct naming pattern for this case (oxo + oic acid), so 'none of these' doesn't apply.

short: Acetic acid is a weaker acid than sulfuric acid mainly because it has a much lower degree of ionization in water.
long: Sulfuric acid is a strong acid that ionizes essentially completely in water, while acetic acid is a weak acid that only partially dissociates into ions (establishing an equilibrium rather than going to completion). This difference in the extent (degree) of ionization is the direct reason acetic acid behaves as a weaker acid overall.
trick: The -COOH group and inductive effects influence HOW acidic a molecule is at a structural level, but the direct, defining reason acetic acid is classified as 'weak' rather than 'strong' is specifically its incomplete (low) degree of ionization in solution.

options.a: Thermal decomposition on heating isn't what defines an acid as weak versus strong.
options.b: Correct — acetic acid's lower degree of ionization compared to sulfuric acid is why it's classified as weak.
options.c: Having a -COOH group is a structural feature, but doesn't by itself explain the weak/strong distinction being tested here.
options.d: More inductive effect would tend to strengthen, not weaken, an acid — this doesn't correctly explain the comparison.

short: Acetic acid reacting with thionyl chloride (SOCl2) produces acetyl chloride, along with sulfur dioxide and hydrogen chloride gas byproducts.
long: Thionyl chloride is a classic reagent for converting carboxylic acids into acid chlorides. Acetic acid (CH3COOH) reacts with SOCl2 to form acetyl chloride (CH3COCl), releasing SO2 and HCl gases as byproducts — a clean, commonly used method since both byproducts leave as gases, simplifying purification of the product.
trick: SOCl2 is specifically known for this exact transformation (carboxylic acid → acid chloride + SO2 + HCl) — memorize this reagent-to-product pattern, since it shows up repeatedly across organic chemistry questions.

options.a: Correct — acetic acid + thionyl chloride gives acetyl chloride, releasing SO2 and HCl gases.
options.b: This product set doesn't match the actual thionyl chloride reaction with a carboxylic acid.
options.c: This would resemble an esterification product, not what SOCl2 produces with a carboxylic acid.
options.d: This product set doesn't include the acid chloride, which is the actual expected product of this reaction.

short: Protein digestion, just before absorption, yields a mixture of amino acids and small polypeptides (di- and tripeptides).
long: Digestive enzymes (pepsin, trypsin, chymotrypsin, and intestinal peptidases) progressively break dietary protein down, but digestion doesn't reduce everything all the way to single amino acids before absorption begins — a substantial portion is absorbed as small peptides (di- and tripeptides) via specific transporters, alongside free amino acids.
trick: It's a common oversimplification to think digestion must go 'all the way' to individual amino acids before absorption — in reality, the intestine absorbs a mix of free amino acids AND small peptides.

options.a: Correct — both amino acids and small polypeptides are present just before absorption, and both get absorbed.
options.b: This ignores the real contribution of small peptide absorption alongside free amino acids.
options.c: Digestion does break most protein down further than just polypeptides — free amino acids are present too.
options.d: Ammonia isn't a direct digestion product of dietary protein at this stage.

short: Dehydrating an alcohol with concentrated H2SO4 at a lower temperature (~140°C), with excess alcohol, favors intermolecular dehydration to give an ether (diethyl ether from ethanol).
long: Alcohol dehydration with sulfuric acid is temperature-dependent: at a lower temperature (~140°C) with excess alcohol present, intermolecular dehydration dominates, joining two alcohol molecules together (losing water) to form an ether. At a higher temperature (~170°C) with excess acid, intramolecular dehydration instead dominates, forming an alkene.
trick: The exact temperature matters here — 140°C is specifically the lower-temperature condition favoring ether formation; if the temperature given were higher (~170°C), the product would instead be an alkene, not an ether.

options.a: Acetaldehyde would come from oxidation of an alcohol, not from acid-catalyzed dehydration.
options.b: Correct — at ~140°C with H2SO4 and excess alcohol, intermolecular dehydration gives diethyl ether.
options.c: Ethyl acetate would require an esterification reaction with a carboxylic acid, not simple dehydration.
options.d: Ethyl chloride would require a halogenating reagent (like HCl or SOCl2), not sulfuric acid dehydration.

short: Complete oxidation of a (primary) alcohol yields a carboxylic acid.
long: Primary alcohols oxidize in two stages: partial oxidation gives an aldehyde, while complete (further) oxidation pushes the aldehyde on to a carboxylic acid. This is why controlling reaction conditions (like using a mild oxidant and removing the aldehyde as it forms via distillation) is necessary if you want to isolate the aldehyde rather than let oxidation proceed all the way.
trick: Aldehyde is the product of PARTIAL oxidation — since this question specifically asks about COMPLETE oxidation, the reaction goes one step further, all the way to the carboxylic acid.

options.a: Aldehyde is the partial oxidation product — complete oxidation goes one step further.
options.b: Alkane formation isn't a product of alcohol oxidation at all.
options.c: Correct — complete oxidation of a primary alcohol yields a carboxylic acid.
options.d: Ketone formation is what happens with secondary (not primary) alcohol oxidation, and even then, it doesn't proceed further to a carboxylic acid.

short: Le Chatelier's principle is used to predict the direction an equilibrium will shift in response to a change in conditions.
long: Le Chatelier's principle states that a system at equilibrium responds to any imposed change (in concentration, pressure, or temperature) by shifting in the direction that counteracts that change — making it the standard tool for predicting which way an equilibrium will move. The law of mass action instead relates rate to concentration, and doesn't directly predict shift direction the same way.
trick: The law of mass action is easy to confuse with Le Chatelier's principle since both deal with equilibrium concepts, but mass action defines the equilibrium expression itself, while Le Chatelier's principle is specifically the tool for predicting shift direction after a disturbance.

options.a: Correct — Le Chatelier's principle predicts the direction of an equilibrium shift.
options.b: The law of mass action describes the equilibrium expression/rate relationship, not shift direction prediction directly.
options.c: This isn't a standard recognized law relevant to equilibrium shift prediction.
options.d: Heat of formation relates to a compound's formation energy, not equilibrium shift direction.

short: The H-H bond energy in a hydrogen molecule is 436 kJ/mol, a standard reference value.
long: The bond dissociation energy of H2 — the energy required to break one mole of H-H bonds into individual hydrogen atoms — is a well-established reference value of 436 kJ/mol, commonly cited in thermochemistry problems involving bond energy calculations (like Hess's law-based enthalpy estimates).
trick: This is a value worth simply memorizing as a standard reference figure (like other common bond energies), since it appears repeatedly across thermochemistry-style questions.

options.a: This value is lower than the actual, standard H-H bond energy.
options.b: This value is close to, but doesn't match the standard, commonly cited figure for H-H bond energy.
options.c: Correct — 436 kJ/mol is the standard reference bond energy for H2.
options.d: This value is different from the standard figure typically used for the H-H bond in H2.

short: Vinyl alcohol and acetaldehyde are tautomers of each other — different structural arrangements in rapid equilibrium.
long: Vinyl alcohol (CH2=CH-OH, an enol) and acetaldehyde (CH3-CHO, a ketone/aldehyde form) have the same molecular formula but differ in the position of a hydrogen atom and a double bond, interconverting rapidly via keto-enol tautomerism. Acetaldehyde is overwhelmingly favored at equilibrium, but the two structures are classified as tautomers, not simply isomers of a fixed, static type.
trick: Tautomers are a special, dynamic case of structural isomerism (they interconvert rapidly and exist in equilibrium) — don't lump them in with static isomer categories like position or chain isomers, which don't spontaneously interconvert the same way.

options.a: Position isomers have a fixed structural difference and don't dynamically interconvert the way tautomers do.
options.b: Chain isomers differ in their carbon skeleton, which isn't the case here — these two share the same base structure differing only in the O-H/C-H and double bond position.
options.c: Metamers involve different alkyl groups on either side of a functional group, a different (static) isomer type.
options.d: Correct — vinyl alcohol and acetaldehyde are keto-enol tautomers, dynamically interconverting.

short: Any free (uncombined) element, including magnesium, has an oxidation number of 0.
long: By definition, an atom in its elemental (uncombined) form — not bonded to a different element — has an oxidation number of zero, since there's no electron transfer or unequal sharing to assign. This applies universally to any free element, including metals like magnesium in its native metallic form.
trick: This is a basic, universal oxidation-number rule that applies to every element in its free state — don't overthink it by trying to apply magnesium's 'usual' +2 oxidation state, which only applies once it's bonded/combined with something else.

options.a: Correct — the oxidation number of any free (uncombined) element is always 0.
options.b: +1 isn't magnesium's typical oxidation state in any common context, combined or free.
options.c: +2 is magnesium's oxidation state when combined in a compound, not in its free elemental form.
options.d: +3 isn't a real oxidation state magnesium takes in any common context.

short: Aluminum (Al) is the metal extracted from the ore bauxite.
long: Bauxite, primarily composed of aluminum oxide (Al2O3) along with impurities, is the principal commercial ore of aluminum. It's refined via the Bayer process to obtain pure alumina, which is then electrolytically reduced (Hall-Héroult process) to produce metallic aluminum.
trick: This is a straightforward ore-to-metal recall fact — bauxite is specifically and uniquely associated with aluminum extraction in standard chemistry curricula.

options.a: Correct — bauxite is the principal ore from which aluminum is extracted.
options.b: Calcium isn't extracted from bauxite — it comes from ores like limestone/gypsum-related sources.
options.c: Magnesium isn't extracted from bauxite — it comes from other sources like magnesite or seawater.
options.d: Copper isn't extracted from bauxite — it comes from sulfide ores like chalcopyrite.

short: Alkali metals have the largest atomic radius in their respective periods, compared to the other groups listed.
long: Atomic radius decreases across a period from left to right, as increasing nuclear charge pulls the electron cloud in tighter without adding new shells. Alkali metals sit at the far left (Group 1) of each period, giving them the largest atomic radius in their row compared to alkaline earth metals, chalcogens, or halogens, which lie progressively further right.
trick: Don't confuse 'largest radius in a period' with 'largest radius in a group' — down a group, radius increases, but across a period (left to right), it's the leftmost group (alkali metals) that has the largest atoms.

options.a: Alkaline earth metals (Group 2) are smaller than alkali metals (Group 1) in the same period, since they're one step further right.
options.b: Correct — alkali metals, being furthest left in their period, have the largest atomic radius among these groups.
options.c: Chalcogens (Group 16) are much further right in the period, and correspondingly smaller.
options.d: Halogens (Group 17) are even further right, and among the smallest atoms in their period.

short: The configuration 1s² 2s² 2p¹ (boron, 5 electrons) belongs to Group IIIA.
long: Group IIIA (13) elements have an outermost electron configuration of ns²np¹ — three valence electrons total. Among the given options, 1s² 2s² 2p¹ (5 electrons total, matching boron) fits this ns²np¹ pattern, correctly placing it in Group IIIA.
trick: Count total valence electrons in the outermost shell carefully (2 in s + 1 in p = 3 valence electrons) — that's the signature of Group IIIA, distinct from options with 2, 3, or 4 electrons in the 2p subshell (which would belong to different groups).

options.b: This configuration's exact subscript is garbled in the source, but it doesn't match the correct Group IIIA pattern.
options.c: Correct — 1s² 2s² 2p¹ (3 valence electrons, ns²np¹ pattern) is boron, in Group IIIA.
options.d: This configuration doesn't match the ns²np¹ (Group IIIA) valence pattern.

short: Alkali metal chlorides (like NaCl, KCl) dissolve in water to give neutral solutions, at pH 7.
long: Salts formed from a strong base (like an alkali metal hydroxide) and a strong acid (like HCl) are neutral salts — neither the alkali metal cation nor the chloride anion undergoes significant hydrolysis in water, so the resulting solution remains at neutral pH 7, just like pure water.
trick: It's tempting to assume any 'metal chloride' might be acidic given how reactive some metal ions can be, but alkali metal ions specifically are very weak Lewis acids (they don't hydrolyze water noticeably), which is why their chloride salts stay neutral rather than acidic or basic.

options.a: Alkali metal chlorides are quite soluble in water, not insoluble.
options.b: Correct — alkali metal chlorides (from strong base + strong acid) give neutral, pH 7 solutions.
options.c: An acidic solution would result if the cation were a stronger Lewis acid (as with some transition metal chlorides), which alkali metals are not.
options.d: A strongly alkaline solution isn't produced by these salts — the strong-acid/strong-base combination gives a neutral solution, not a basic one.

short: Beryllium oxide (BeO) is amphoteric — it can react with both acids and bases.
long: Beryllium, due to its small size and diagonal relationship with aluminum, shows unusually covalent, amphoteric-like chemistry unlike the rest of its group (Group 2 alkaline earth metals, which typically form basic oxides). BeO can react with both acids (acting as a base) and bases (acting as an acid), a property it shares with its diagonal neighbor aluminum oxide, unlike the straightforwardly basic oxides of lithium, calcium, and potassium.
trick: Beryllium is the classic 'exception' element in its group due to the diagonal relationship with aluminum — remember this specific exception pattern whenever a question tests amphoteric behavior among alkaline/alkali metal oxides.

options.a: Lithium oxide is a basic oxide, not amphoteric.
options.b: Correct — beryllium oxide is amphoteric, due to beryllium's diagonal relationship with aluminum.
options.c: Calcium oxide is a straightforwardly basic oxide, not amphoteric.
options.d: Potassium oxide is a strongly basic oxide, not amphoteric.

short: Fe²⁺ (iron(II) ion) has the configuration [Ar]4s⁰3d⁶ — the two 4s electrons are lost first when iron forms this ion.
long: Neutral iron (Z=26) is [Ar]4s²3d⁶. When forming a cation, transition metals lose their outermost (4s) electrons before any 3d electrons, since 4s becomes higher in energy than 3d once the atom is ionized. So Fe²⁺ loses both 4s electrons, giving [Ar]3d⁶ (i.e. 4s⁰3d⁶), not a configuration that removed d electrons instead.
trick: It's a common mistake to think electrons are removed in the reverse order they were added (which would remove 3d electrons first) — but for transition metal cations, 4s electrons are always removed before 3d electrons, regardless of filling order.

options.a: Correct — Fe²⁺ loses its two 4s electrons first, giving [Ar]4s⁰3d⁶.
options.b: This configuration incorrectly keeps both 4s electrons, which shouldn't remain once the +2 ion forms.
options.c: This configuration incorrectly keeps both 4s electrons and removes d electrons instead — the opposite of the actual ionization pattern.
options.d: This configuration doesn't correctly balance to the +2 charge with the right electron count removed from the right subshell.

short: Ethyl acetate contains an ester functional group.
long: Ethyl acetate (CH3-CO-O-CH2CH3) is formed from the condensation of acetic acid and ethanol, joined through a C(=O)-O-C linkage — the defining structure of an ester functional group. This is distinct from a simple ether (C-O-C, no carbonyl), an aldehyde, or a standalone carboxyl group.
trick: Don't mistake the ester's C(=O)-O-C linkage for a simple ether (just C-O-C) — the carbonyl group fused with the oxygen bridge is specifically what makes it an ester, not an ether.

options.a: There's no free aldehyde C-H present in ethyl acetate.
options.b: The carboxyl group has been converted into an ester linkage — it's no longer a free carboxylic acid group.
options.c: Correct — ethyl acetate's C(=O)-O-C linkage is the defining ester functional group.
options.d: An ether lacks the carbonyl (C=O) that's present in ethyl acetate's actual ester linkage.

short: Pyridine's molecular formula is C5H5N.
long: Pyridine is a six-membered aromatic ring like benzene, but with one CH replaced by a nitrogen atom. This substitution gives it 5 carbons (each bearing one hydrogen) plus the ring nitrogen, for a molecular formula of C5H5N — one nitrogen taking the 'CH' spot benzene would otherwise have (C6H6 minus one CH, plus N).
trick: Think of pyridine as 'benzene with one CH swapped for N' — that mental shortcut correctly gets you from C6H6 to C5H5N without needing to redraw the whole ring from scratch.

short: Alkynes are commonly prepared by double dehydrohalogenation (elimination of two HX molecules) from a vicinal dihalide, using excess strong base.
long: Starting from a vicinal dihalide (two halogens on adjacent carbons), treatment with excess strong base (like alcoholic KOH or sodamide, NaNH2) removes two molecules of HX in sequence, forming first an alkene-halide intermediate and then the alkyne — the standard textbook method for alkyne synthesis from dihalides.
trick: This is a case where two options both mention 'dehalogenation of vicinal dihalides,' differing only in the reaction conditions listed (methanol vs. strong base) — the mechanistically correct condition for this classic elimination is a strong base (like alcoholic KOH), not a simple alcohol solvent like methanol alone.

options.a: Methanol alone isn't a strong enough base/conditions to drive this double elimination to an alkyne.
options.b: Alcohol dehydration with alumina is a method for making alkenes from alcohols, not alkynes from dihalides.
options.c: This describes the standard double-elimination method (strong base) for alkyne synthesis from a vicinal dihalide — a commonly cited alternative to the stored answer.
options.d: Electrolysis of dicarboxylic acid salts is the answer recorded in the source material for this question, though the double-dehydrohalogenation route (option C) is the more standard textbook method — treat this one as a case where either could be defensible depending on the reference used.
